Home / Industries / Aggregates, Quarries and Cement Industry Aggregates, Quarries and Cement Magnetic Separator Applications Selection support for crusher protection and material stream cleanup in aggregate, quarry and cement processes. Industry overview Selection support for crusher protection and material stream cleanup in aggregate, quarry and cement processes. Common operating conditions Dust, heat and outdoor installation may apply Heavy material loads and large lump sizes require confirmation Remote mining sites may need spare parts planning Typical tramp iron problems Bolts, tools, teeth, wire and ferrous debris can damage conveyors, crushers and processing equipment. Risks to crushers and conveyors Unremoved tramp iron may cut belts, block transfer points, damage crusher liners, interrupt production and increase maintenance risk. Recommended magnetic equipment Suspended permanent magnets, self-cleaning overband separators, electromagnetic separators and magnetic pulleys may be reviewed. Installation methods Cross-belt and inline positions should be checked against transfer points, belt speed, burden depth, maintenance access and available structure. Product selection factors Material type and maximum lump size Conveyor width, speed and layer depth Suspension height Manual or self-cleaning discharge Outdoor, dusty, humid or corrosive conditions Review your application Send the material, conveyor and installation data required for a project-specific equipment review. Request a Quote Recommended products Equipment families commonly reviewed for this process. Final selection depends on verified operating data. Magnetic Separation Equipment Suspended Permanent Magnetic Separator Suspended Permanent Magnetic Separator is presented as a suspended magnetic separator option for conveyor and bulk material handling. Its final configuration should be based on the actual material, process position, operating conditions and the technical information available for the requested project. Magnetic Separation Equipment Suspended Electromagnetic Conveyor Belt Separator Suspended Electromagnetic Conveyor Belt Separator is presented as a suspended magnetic separator option for conveyor and bulk material handling. Its final configuration should be based on the actual material, process position, operating conditions and the technical information available for the requested project. Industry Application Equipment Round Electromagnetic Lifting Magnet Round Electromagnetic Lifting Magnet is presented as a electromagnetic lifting magnet option for ferrous material handling. Its final configuration should be based on the actual material, process position, operating conditions and the technical information available for the requested project. Related solutions Explore process problems that magnetic separation and metal detection can help address. Solution Conveyor Protection Reduce the risk of belt damage, transfer-point blockages and downstream equipment disruption from tramp metal and unsuitable material separation. Solution Non-Ferrous Metal Recovery Review prepared material, particle size, feed presentation and downstream collection for non-ferrous separation. Solution Tramp Iron Removal Remove ferrous tramp metal before it reaches crushers, screens or process equipment. FAQ Which separator type is recommended? The product family depends on conveyor data, burden depth, tramp iron risk and duty cycle. Can this be used in dusty sites? Dust protection and outdoor configuration must be confirmed for each site.

Product FAQ Questions buyers ask Answers apply to this product family and do not replace a project-specific engineering review. When is self-cleaning preferred over manual cleaning? Self-cleaning is normally considered where ferrous contamination must be discharged continuously. Manual cleaning may be appropriate when contamination is low and the line can be isolated safely for service. Should the magnet be installed inline or cross-belt? The installation direction depends on belt speed, burden depth, the discharge side, available headroom and the required exposure to the magnetic field. The conveyor arrangement should be reviewed before selection. What information is needed for a suspended magnet quote? Please provide belt width, speed, material layer depth, suspension height, material description, the largest expected tramp item, desired cleaning method and a layout drawing or photos when available. Can this separator remove all metals? No. A magnetic separator is used for ferromagnetic contaminants. Non-ferrous metals and non-magnetic stainless steel require a different separation or detection stage. Self-cleaning is normally considered where ferrous contamination must be discharged continuously. Manual cleaning may be appropriate when contamination is low and the line can be isolated safely for service. Should the magnet be installed inline or cross-belt? The installation direction depends on belt speed, burden depth, the discharge side, available headroom and the required exposure to the magnetic field. The conveyor arrangement should be reviewed before selection. What information is needed for a suspended magnet quote? Please provide belt width, speed, material layer depth, suspension height, material description, the largest expected tramp item, desired cleaning method and a layout drawing or photos when available. Can this separator remove all metals? No. A magnetic separator is used for ferromagnetic contaminants. Non-ferrous metals and non-magnetic stainless steel require a different separation or detection stage. Product FAQ Questions buyers ask Answers apply to this product family and do not replace a project-specific engineering review. When is self-cleaning preferred over manual cleaning? Self-cleaning is normally considered where ferrous contamination must be discharged continuously. Manual cleaning may be appropriate when contamination is low and the line can be isolated safely for service. Should the magnet be installed inline or cross-belt? The installation direction depends on belt speed, burden depth, the discharge side, available headroom and the required exposure to the magnetic field. The conveyor arrangement should be reviewed before selection. What information is needed for a suspended magnet quote? Please provide belt width, speed, material layer depth, suspension height, material description, the largest expected tramp item, desired cleaning method and a layout drawing or photos when available. Can this separator remove all metals? No. A magnetic separator is used for ferromagnetic contaminants. Non-ferrous metals and non-magnetic stainless steel require a different separation or detection stage. Product FAQ Questions buyers ask Answers apply to this product family and do not replace a project-specific engineering review. When is self-cleaning preferred over manual cleaning? Self-cleaning is normally considered where ferrous contamination must be discharged continuously. Manual cleaning may be appropriate when contamination is low and the line can be isolated safely for service. Should the magnet be installed inline or cross-belt? The installation direction depends on belt speed, burden depth, the discharge side, available headroom and the required exposure to the magnetic field. The conveyor arrangement should be reviewed before selection. What information is needed for a suspended magnet quote? Please provide belt width, speed, material layer depth, suspension height, material description, the largest expected tramp item, desired cleaning method and a layout drawing or photos when available. Can this separator remove all metals? No. A magnetic separator is used for ferromagnetic contaminants. Non-ferrous metals and non-magnetic stainless steel require a different separation or detection stage. Product FAQ Questions buyers ask Answers apply to this product family and do not replace a project-specific engineering review. Which magnetic filter is suitable for dry powder or pellets? The choice depends on free-flowing behavior, particle size, available headroom and cleaning access. Drawer, grid and bar arrangements are commonly reviewed for gravity-flow duties. Can a magnetic filter replace a metal detector? No. A magnetic filter captures ferromagnetic particles. A metal detector is a detection system and may identify other metals depending on its configuration. What should be confirmed for liquid or slurry filtration? Please provide flow rate, viscosity, temperature, solids content, line pressure, connection size, installation orientation and the expected contamination type. Does every magnetic filter meet food-processing requirements? No. Food-related contact material, finish, cleaning method and documentation must be confirmed for the actual process; they should not be assumed from a product family name. Home / Blog / Guide Selection Guide Conveyor Belt Magnetic Separators for South African Mines Learn how South African mines choose conveyor belt magnetic separators for tramp iron removal, crusher protection, belt width and burden depth. Published: 2026-07-06 - Updated: 2026-08-08 - Author: Cowin Magnet South Africa A conveyor belt magnetic separator is used above or near a conveyor to remove ferrous tramp metal before it damages crushers, screens, transfer chutes, mills or downstream process equipment. For South African mines, the main buying question is not simply which magnet is strongest. The real question is which separator can reach the tramp iron through the actual material burden, fit the conveyor layout, discharge metal safely and operate reliably in the mine environment. This guide is written for mining plants, quarry operators, coal handling sites, cement raw material lines and mineral processing projects in South Africa and wider African markets. It explains how to choose between overband, suspended permanent and suspended electromagnetic conveyor belt magnetic separators, what data to prepare before quotation, and which mistakes commonly lead to poor separation results. Key Takeaways Selection depends on belt width, burden depth, suspension height, belt speed, material type and tramp iron size. Self-cleaning overband magnets are usually preferred where tramp metal appears frequently or conveyor uptime is critical. Permanent magnets suit many standard conveyor protection duties; electromagnetic separators may be reviewed for deeper burden or adjustable force requirements. Installation position and discharge path are as important as magnetic strength. A proper quote should be based on operating data, not only a photo or belt width. Magnetic separators remove ferrous metal; non-ferrous detection or recovery may need other equipment. Use Case: Conveyor Protection in South African Mines South African mining sites often handle abrasive material, long conveyors, variable feed rates and large lumps from primary crushing or ROM stockpiles. Ferrous tramp metal can come from bucket teeth, drill rods, liner fragments, bolts, screen parts, tools, wire rope and conveyor hardware. If these pieces reach a crusher or screen, they can cause belt damage, blocked chutes, broken liners, emergency shutdowns and unplanned maintenance. A conveyor belt magnetic separator is installed to remove magnetic ferrous metal from the conveyed material stream. In practical terms, it acts as a protection device for mechanical equipment and a contamination-control device for the process. It can be used before jaw crushers, cone crushers, impact crushers, secondary crushers, screens, transfer stations, coal handling conveyors, aggregate lines and recycling feed belts. Recommended Equipment Types The most common choice for continuous conveyor tramp iron removal is an overband magnetic separator. It is suspended over the belt and usually includes a self-cleaning discharge belt that carries captured metal away from the main material flow. This makes it suitable for mines where stopping the conveyor for cleaning is not practical. A suspended permanent magnetic separator may be suitable where the contamination level is low and manual cleaning is acceptable. It can be simple and effective when the burden depth is manageable and the magnet can be installed close enough to the material. A suspended electromagnetic conveyor belt separator may be considered when the plant needs adjustable magnetic force or when the burden depth and suspension height require a stronger field review. For some sites, a magnetic head pulley or drum magnet may also be reviewed at discharge points. These are not direct substitutes for every overband magnet application, but they can be useful where the conveyor layout and material trajectory allow separation at the pulley or transfer point. Key Selection Parameters The first parameter is belt width. The magnetic field must cover the actual material stream, including off-centre loading if the conveyor is not evenly loaded. A separator selected only from nominal belt width may miss material concentrated on one side of the belt. The second parameter is burden depth, which is the thickness of material on the conveyor. A shallow burden is easier for the magnet to penetrate. A deep burden can hide tramp iron under a layer of ore, coal or aggregate. This is one of the most common reasons a magnet that looks large enough on paper performs poorly at site. The third parameter is suspension height. Magnetic force drops as the distance from the magnet face increases. The separator should be installed with enough clearance for safe material flow but close enough to attract tramp iron. Other important parameters include belt speed, capacity per hour, material lump size, moisture level, material density, installation angle, power availability and expected tramp iron size. Permanent vs Electromagnetic Separators A permanent magnetic separator uses permanent magnet material and does not need electrical power to create the magnetic field. For many South African conveyor protection applications, this can be practical because the magnetic field is always available and the system is relatively simple. A self-cleaning permanent overband magnet still needs a motor for the cleaning belt, but not for the magnetic field itself. An electromagnetic separator uses an energized coil. It may be reviewed when the application needs higher magnetic reach, adjustable operating conditions or site-specific control. The trade-off is that it requires reliable power, controls and maintenance attention. It should not be chosen only because it sounds more powerful. The right choice depends on the burden depth, suspension height, duty cycle and site conditions. Self-Cleaning vs Manual-Cleaning A self-cleaning separator is usually preferred where tramp metal appears regularly. The continuous cleaning belt removes captured metal from the magnetic zone and discharges it to the side of the conveyor. This helps keep the conveyor running and reduces the need for operators to stop the line for manual cleaning. A manual-cleaning suspended magnet can still be suitable for lighter-duty or occasional-contamination applications. It may fit smaller conveyors, temporary installations or sites where inspection and cleaning are easy to schedule. The decision should consider safety procedures, production pressure, the frequency of tramp iron and the physical access around the conveyor. Common Selection Mistakes One mistake is selecting only by belt width. Belt width is necessary, but it does not describe material depth, lump size, feed rate or magnet height. Two conveyors with the same width can require different separator sizes. Another mistake is ignoring the discharge side. Removed metal must be dropped into a safe collection zone. If there is no space for discharge, the installation may create a maintenance hazard or cause metal to fall back into the material stream. A third mistake is assuming the magnet will remove all metal. Magnetic separators remove ferrous magnetic material. They do not solve non-ferrous contamination, stainless steel detection or every process quality issue. If the risk includes non-ferrous metal, the plant should review metal detectors or eddy current separators separately. Installation and Maintenance Notes Installation should consider structural support, vibration, conveyor guarding, access platforms, lifting clearance, chute design and collection bins. The magnet should be positioned where the material is stable enough for separation and before the equipment that needs protection. Routine maintenance should include checking the self-cleaning belt, bearings, motor, guards, suspension frame, discharge area and collected metal bin. For electromagnetic models, electrical controls and cooling arrangements should also be inspected. In dusty, wet, coastal or high-temperature environments, protection level and corrosion resistance should be discussed before final selection. When This Product Is Suitable A conveyor belt magnetic separator is suitable when ferrous tramp metal may be mixed with ore, coal, aggregate, limestone, recycled material or other conveyed bulk solids. It is particularly relevant before crushers, screens, transfer stations and process equipment that would be expensive to repair after metal impact. It is also suitable when the buyer wants a continuous, visible protection point that can be inspected by maintenance teams. Mines, quarries, cement plants, coal handling systems and recycling plants can all use this type of equipment when the material stream and installation conditions are appropriate. When This Product Is Not Suitable This product is not suitable as the only solution for non-ferrous metal removal. Aluminium, copper and brass require different separation or detection methods. It may also be unsuitable if the burden depth is too high, the magnet must be mounted too far from the material, or the conveyor layout prevents safe discharge of captured metal. If the plant cannot confirm source publication data, operating conditions or material characteristics, equipment selection should remain preliminary. A responsible supplier should request operating data before making a firm recommendation. Information Needed Before Quotation Before requesting a quote, send clear operating data. This allows Cowin Magnet to recommend whether a permanent overband magnet, suspended permanent magnet, electromagnetic separator or another configuration should be reviewed. It also reduces the risk of undersizing or overcomplicating the solution. Quotation Checklist Material type Particle size Moisture level Capacity per hour Conveyor belt width Belt speed Burden depth Installation height Tramp iron size Cleaning method Power availability Working environment FAQ What is a conveyor belt magnetic separator used for in a mine? It is used to remove ferrous tramp metal from material moving on a conveyor before it reaches crushers, screens, mills or other process equipment. In South African mining conditions, it is commonly considered for coal, iron ore, manganese, chrome, gold, quarry stone and aggregate conveyors where steel fragments can damage equipment or cause unplanned shutdowns. Should a South African mine choose a permanent or electromagnetic separator? A permanent separator is often suitable for standard tramp iron removal where the burden depth and installation height are within the magnetic reach of the selected model. An electromagnetic separator may be reviewed when the burden is deeper, the suspension height is higher, or adjustable magnetic force is required. The correct choice depends on site data rather than the country or industry alone. Where should the separator be installed on the conveyor? The usual location is before the crusher, screen or transfer point that needs protection. It may be installed cross-belt or inline depending on the conveyor layout and discharge path. The installation should allow safe clearance above the material, enough space for removed metal to discharge, and practical maintenance access around the magnet and support frame. Can a conveyor belt magnet remove all metal contamination? No. A conveyor belt magnetic separator removes ferrous magnetic metal. It will not remove most aluminium, copper, brass or weakly magnetic stainless steel. If the plant also needs non-ferrous metal recovery or detection, eddy current separation or metal detection may need to be reviewed as a separate part of the process. What information is needed before requesting a quote? Send material type, particle size, moisture, capacity per hour, belt width, belt speed, burden depth, installation height, tramp iron size, preferred cleaning method, power availability and working environment. Photos or drawings of the conveyor are also useful. Without this data, a supplier can only provide a rough recommendation. Is a self-cleaning separator necessary? Self-cleaning is recommended when tramp iron appears frequently, when the conveyor runs for long shifts, or when stopping the belt for manual cleaning would reduce production. Manual-cleaning suspended magnets can be suitable when contamination is rare and site procedures allow safe cleaning. The decision should consider uptime, safety and maintenance access. Conclusion Choosing a conveyor belt magnetic separator for South African mines requires more than matching a catalog model to belt width. The correct recommendation depends on the material, burden depth, belt speed, installation height, tramp iron risk, cleaning method and site environment. Cowin Magnet can review the application and recommend a suitable magnetic separator configuration for quotation. Published: 2026-09-28 Updated: 2026-09-28 Author: Cowin Magnet South Africa Editorial Team COWIN product image; final configuration is project-specific. Key Takeaways What the recorded sources say The current source set consists of Mining Weekly: “Big boost for platinum, palladium as China exchange internationalises”; Statistics South Africa: “GDP declines by 0,2% in Q2: 2026”. These public updates provide context for South African industry and project planning. They do not identify a COWIN customer, purchase, local stockholding or operating result, and they do not establish that one magnetic separator configuration suits any named project. The engineering value of the sources is to prompt a disciplined review of material flow, equipment interfaces and the information required before a supplier can confirm selection. This article therefore separates reported context from COWIN's process-selection guidance. Source titles, publishers, links and dates are retained for traceability. The discussion below is an original engineering interpretation and does not reproduce the source articles or infer commercial relationships. Convert a broad industry update into a defined plant question An industry announcement is useful context, not a purchase specification. A plant review should identify the material route, the downstream equipment exposed to ferrous contamination and the consequence of an undetected object. That information establishes whether the immediate need is detection, removal, process separation or a combination of controls. It also prevents general market news from being presented as evidence of a specific customer project, local installation or guaranteed performance. Locate the protection point from process evidence The proposed position should be checked against burden depth, material trajectory, belt speed, headroom, nearby steelwork and the route available for captured metal. A convenient open space is not automatically the best separation point. Drawings and clear photographs help identify structural and maintenance constraints, while operating records can show where contamination becomes visible and which downstream machine experiences the greatest consequence. Match cleaning method to the operating pattern Manual-cleaning and self-cleaning systems serve different production conditions. The review should consider contamination frequency, whether the process can stop safely, where removed metal will be discharged and how personnel will access the equipment. Permanent and electromagnetic magnet systems also have different power, controls and maintenance implications. Those attributes should remain tied to the actual product under review rather than combined into a generic description. Confirm installation geometry early A dimensioned layout should show suspension height, belt profile, transfer trajectory, structural members and the space available for discharge and maintenance. Nearby steel can influence the arrangement, while insufficient headroom can make a nominal equipment selection impractical. Reviewing the geometry before order placement reduces the risk of site modifications and gives structural designers the loads and access requirements needed for their work. Account for the site environment Outdoor exposure, dust, rainfall, corrosion, ambient temperature and altitude can affect enclosure, coating, cooling and electrical decisions. Coastal and remote locations may also change material choices and the spare-parts strategy. These conditions should be listed explicitly rather than hidden inside a general heavy-duty requirement, allowing the final quotation to state which environmental assumptions are included. Evaluate lifecycle support Selection should consider consumables, wear components, inspection skills, documentation and the time required to obtain replacement parts. Remote operations may prefer arrangements that simplify routine service, while high-throughput plants may place greater weight on continuous cleaning and planned redundancy. Lifecycle discussion should follow technical suitability and should not be used to justify equipment that does not meet the separation duty. Coordinate controls and interlocks Run permissives, belt-speed inputs, local controls, alarms and emergency-stop interfaces should be documented when they form part of the selected configuration. The cause-and-effect description should state what happens during startup, a separator fault, a stopped conveyor and maintenance isolation. Clear boundaries between the equipment package and the plant control system prevent signals from being assumed by both parties or supplied by neither. Prepare commissioning evidence Before startup, teams should confirm installation dimensions, rotation and discharge direction, electrical checks, guarding, isolation and the condition of the material path. Commissioning records should capture the operating settings and any controlled test used to confirm function. Training should cover normal inspection, abnormal events and who owns follow-up actions. These records become the reference for later troubleshooting. Define the downstream consequence The protected asset may be a crusher, screen, mill, conveyor or product stream, and each has a different consequence when unwanted metal passes. The team should describe credible events and the operating response expected after detection or capture. This focuses the selection discussion on risk reduction and availability rather than treating magnetic strength or belt width as a complete specification. Where Permanent Overband Magnetic Separator may fit Permanent Overband Magnetic Separator may be reviewed where its actual magnet system, cleaning method and installation arrangement match the confirmed duty. It is not a universal answer and no performance value should be inferred from this article. COWIN engineering would require the design basis, layout and operating objective before confirming a model, working position or project-specific capability. The product record and quotation must describe only the configuration under review. Questions to resolve before a quotation Can equipment be selected from conveyor width alone? No. Width is one input. Burden depth, belt speed, suspension height, material behaviour, contamination, cleaning requirements, surrounding steelwork and downstream risk must also be reviewed. Does the source announcement prove that a magnetic separator is required? No. It provides industry context. The need and configuration must come from the process objective and verified site information. What should the buyer send first? Send a concise process description, dimensioned layout or photographs, material and throughput information, observed contamination details, environmental conditions and the downstream equipment or product-quality objective that requires protection. Practical next steps Confirm the process objective and the consequence of unwanted metal. Measure the material and installation conditions at the proposed position. Define cleaning, discharge, controls, access and environmental requirements. Record assumptions and assign owners for missing information. Request a project-specific review before treating provisional data as a guarantee. Key Takeaways What the public update establishes Recent public statements describe illegal mining as a criminal and economic risk to South Africa's formal mining sector. That is the verified news context for this article. The sources do not identify a COWIN customer, installation or equipment purchase, and they do not establish that magnetic separation alone can address illegal mining. Their practical value for plant teams is narrower: they highlight why traceability, controlled material movement and clearly assigned operating responsibility matter throughout a mineral-handling chain. For mine, contractor and processing teams, material security is not confined to a boundary fence. Unauthorised extraction or uncontrolled feed can affect what reaches stockpiles, transfer points and processing equipment. Each operation requires its own security, legal and operating controls. Equipment selection should support those controls without being presented as a substitute for law enforcement, access management, sampling, reconciliation or responsible procurement. Where material-control questions enter the process A useful review starts by mapping custody from the point where material is received or reclaimed to the point where it enters a crusher, screen, plant feed system or final product stream. Teams should identify who authorises each transfer, how unusual loads are isolated, where samples are taken and how discrepancies are recorded. This makes abnormal events visible before they are treated as routine production variation. The review should distinguish three different issues: unauthorised material, unwanted ferrous objects and normal process variability. A magnetic separator may help remove suitable ferrous contamination at a defined process position, but it cannot verify legal ownership, mineral origin or commercial grade. Metal detection, sampling, weighing, access control and documentary checks solve different parts of the control problem and should not be collapsed into one equipment claim. Why tramp-metal risk still needs a separate assessment Material from uncontrolled or poorly documented handling can contain tools, wire, fasteners, worn components or other ferrous objects. Similar contamination can also arise in fully authorised operations through maintenance and equipment wear. The source of the object matters for investigation, but separator selection depends on the physical duty: object size and shape, burden depth, conveyor speed, suspension height, material characteristics and the downstream machine that requires protection. Plant teams should therefore keep an event record rather than assuming every captured item has the same origin. Photographs, approximate dimensions, discovery position and operating conditions can help maintenance and security teams identify patterns. The record can also improve later equipment reviews by replacing general statements such as "heavy contamination" with observable information. How a magnetic equipment review fits Permanent Overband Magnetic Separator is one equipment family that may be considered for a conveyor-protection duty when its verified configuration matches the process. It is not a security system and it is not evidence that material is lawful or saleable. COWIN engineering would still need the actual conveyor, burden, contamination, installation and environmental data before confirming a project configuration. The cleaning arrangement must match the expected operating pattern. A self-cleaning system may be reviewed where captured ferrous material must be discharged without routine production stops and where a safe discharge route exists. A manual-cleaning arrangement serves a different duty. Permanent and electromagnetic systems also have different installation, power, control and maintenance considerations; those attributes must remain separated in the selected product record and quotation. Information to collect before selecting equipment Conveyor width, belt speed, maximum burden depth and the proposed separator position. Material type, particle-size range, moisture, temperature and bulk behaviour. Observed ferrous objects, including approximate size, shape, frequency and where they were found. Required cleaning method and the safe route for collected material. Outdoor exposure, dust, corrosion, altitude and electrical supply where relevant. The site's own custody, incident-reporting and isolation procedures for unusual material. Operational controls around the installation An installation review should consider guarding, isolation, inspection access and ownership of collected material. The plant should define who may inspect the separator, who records recovered objects and where those objects are transferred. If an item may be relevant to a security or safety investigation, it should be handled under the site's approved procedure rather than discarded through an informal route. Nearby steelwork and the material trajectory should be checked before finalising the position. A dimensioned layout and clear site photographs are more useful than conveyor width alone. The discharge path must not create a new hazard, obstruct a walkway or return captured objects to the process. These are project-specific engineering questions, not conclusions that can be drawn from a national industry statement. Security staff review custody records while operations map the conveyor positions where contamination becomes visible. Maintenance measures the conveyor, burden and available height, then documents the downstream equipment at risk. The team separately evaluates access controls, sampling and a suitable tramp-metal removal configuration. This approach avoids claiming that one machine solves a broader illegal-mining problem. It cannot determine legal origin, ownership or mineral grade. Does this article describe a COWIN project in South Africa? No. It is an independent engineering interpretation of public information and does not claim a local customer, installation, office or stockholding. Can equipment be selected from belt width alone? No. Burden depth, belt speed, suspension height, material, contamination, installation geometry, cleaning requirements and downstream risk must also be reviewed. What should be recorded after ferrous material is captured? Follow the site's approved procedure. Useful operational details can include time, process position, approximate dimensions, photographs and the route or feed condition associated with the event. Magnetic equipment cannot establish ownership, legality or mineral grade. Selection requires verified process and installation data rather than broad industry assumptions. Captured-material records can support maintenance learning and the site's established security procedures. Published: 2026-08-08 Updated: 2026-08-08 Author: Cowin Magnet South Africa Editorial Team COWIN product image. Configuration must be confirmed against actual process conditions. Key Takeaways Industry updates are context, not evidence of a specific mine's equipment purchase. Conveyor protection selection starts with real material and installation data. A permanent overband configuration should be reviewed against the actual operating conditions. What happened South African mining teams received two useful signals on 23 July 2026. Anglo American's second-quarter production report said that Kumba and Minas-Rio maintained stable operational performance in premium iron ore, while the wider portfolio continued to manage cost and supply-chain pressure. On the same day, the Minerals Council South Africa's Mining Modernisation Showcase brought together mining leaders, policymakers, researchers, labour, technology providers and innovation partners to discuss the sector's future. Neither update is a purchasing announcement for a particular magnetic separator, and neither should be read as evidence of a specific mine configuration. Together, however, they underline a practical point for plant and materials-handling teams: stable production depends on making conveyor protection, maintenance access and selection data part of everyday engineering decisions rather than leaving them until a failure occurs. Where the process is exposed In an iron-ore, manganese, chrome, coal, aggregate or bulk-material circuit, unwanted ferrous tramp metal can enter a conveyor stream through feed contamination, worn equipment, maintenance activity or upstream handling. The exposure is rarely limited to a single transfer point. It can appear before a crusher, at a transfer chute, ahead of a screen, or in a reclaim and stockpile route. The consequence is not automatically a breakdown, but the risk is real enough that the separation point and its maintenance plan should be considered together. Modernisation also makes selection discipline more important. A separator that is physically difficult to inspect, conflicts with a chute, cannot discharge collected material safely, or is selected without confirmed conveyor data can create its own operating burden. A useful project discussion therefore starts with the material path and the constraints around it, not with a generic headline specification. How a magnetic solution fits For conveyor-fed material where continuous removal of ferrous tramp material is required, a permanent overband magnetic separator can be considered as one configuration. The COWIN product catalogue records this family as a permanent magnetic circuit with a self-cleaning discharge arrangement, while final configuration remains subject to actual process conditions. It should not be presented as a universal answer: suitability depends on the material, the conveyor layout, the clearance available and the selected installation arrangement. Where the main decision is protection of downstream equipment, the engineering question is usually whether the magnet is positioned where it can act on the material stream effectively and where collected metal can be removed without creating a secondary hazard. In a recovery application, the objective and downstream material flow may be different. These choices should be kept separate in the quotation and review process. Practical selection checklist Conveyor belt width, belt speed and burden depth at the proposed separation point. Material description, including particle size, moisture, temperature and the type of ferrous contamination to be addressed. Installation position, conveyor direction, available suspension height and structural support information. Whether the process needs manual cleaning or a continuous self-cleaning discharge arrangement. Available discharge space, guard requirements, dust conditions and safe maintenance access. Any upstream metal detector, downstream crusher, screen or other equipment that changes the process objective. Illustrative decision path Illustrative only, not a customer case: a bulk-handling team identifies recurring ferrous contamination before a downstream machine. It first maps the conveyor geometry and operating conditions, then confirms whether the priority is equipment protection or material recovery. If continuous discharge is required and the process supports an overband arrangement, the team can request a configuration review with the belt, burden, clearance and material information listed above. If those inputs are not yet available, the appropriate next step is data collection rather than an unsupported performance claim. Key takeaways Recent South African mining updates reinforce the value of disciplined operating and maintenance decisions, but do not prove a specific product need at any site. Conveyor protection should be assessed from the material path, installation constraints and downstream risk. Permanent and self-cleaning arrangements must be selected against verified project conditions, not mixed into a generic product description. Requesting data before a quotation protects both the buyer and the engineering review. Questions buyers ask Does every conveyor need an overband magnet? No. The need, location and configuration depend on the process objective, contamination risk and physical installation conditions. Can a product be selected from belt width alone? No. Belt width is useful, but burden depth, suspension height, material and conveyor layout also affect the engineering review. Is this article evidence of a COWIN installation at Kumba or another South African mine? No. This is an independent engineering interpretation of public industry updates. It does not claim a customer installation, local office, local stock or local service team. What should be sent with a quote request? Send the conveyor and material details in the selection checklist, together with photographs or a layout drawing where available. Key Takeaways What the latest updates indicate Recent South African mining and industrial updates provide useful context for plant teams reviewing material handling reliability. The reports do not identify a COWIN installation and they do not prove that one equipment configuration suits a named operation. They do, however, reinforce a practical engineering requirement: production plans depend on equipment protection, controlled material flow and maintenance decisions that are based on verified site data. For procurement and engineering teams, the important step is to translate broad industry developments into questions that can be answered at the conveyor, transfer point or process line. That means identifying where unwanted ferrous material can enter the flow, what downstream equipment is exposed, how collected metal can be discharged safely, and which operating conditions affect selection. Where a bulk-material process is exposed Tramp iron may enter mined ore, coal, aggregate or other bulk material through upstream handling, wear, maintenance activity or contaminated feed. A risk point can occur ahead of a crusher, at a transfer chute, before a screen, on a stockpile route or in a reclaim circuit. The consequence varies by process: damage risk, unplanned inspection, contamination or interruption of downstream flow. A magnetic separator should therefore be considered as part of the process layout, not as an isolated catalogue item. Available suspension height, burden depth, belt speed, material characteristics, structural support, discharge space and safe access all influence the review. A configuration that is difficult to inspect or cannot discharge captured material safely can introduce a new operating problem. How magnetic separation can fit Permanent Overband Magnetic Separator is one product family that may be reviewed where its actual cleaning method, magnet system and installation arrangement match the duty. It is not a universal answer. COWIN engineering must confirm the selection against the buyer's material and layout information, and project-specific values remain available on request until that review is complete. The process objective must also be clear. Protecting a downstream crusher is different from recovering a saleable fraction, controlling fine contamination or detecting metal before a critical machine. Keeping these objectives separate helps the project team choose an appropriate equipment family and prevents permanent, electromagnetic, manual-cleaning and self-cleaning attributes from being mixed. Selection information to prepare Conveyor width, belt speed and the maximum burden depth at the proposed position. Material type, particle-size range, moisture, temperature and bulk behaviour. The expected ferrous contamination, including typical shape, size and frequency where known. Installation orientation, suspension height, transfer geometry and available support structure. The downstream machine or product-quality objective that requires protection. Required cleaning method, discharge direction, maintenance access and guarding constraints. Outdoor exposure, dust, corrosion, altitude and the available electrical supply where relevant. Installation and operating review Before quotation, the proposed position should be checked against the material trajectory and nearby steelwork. Photographs and a dimensioned layout are often more useful than a single headline specification. The review should also cover access for inspection, removal of collected metal, guarding, isolation and the route for lifting or replacing wear components. Operating teams should define a realistic inspection routine. The frequency depends on contamination and duty rather than a generic interval. Records of captured material, belt condition and unusual events can improve later configuration decisions without relying on unsupported performance claims. How to compare configuration choices A permanent magnetic system may be considered where the verified duty and installation suit that technology, while an electromagnetic system has different power, control and cooling considerations. Manual-cleaning and self-cleaning arrangements also solve different operating needs. These descriptions must not be combined into one generic specification: the selected product page and quotation should describe only the actual configuration under review. The cleaning decision should account for the amount and frequency of captured material, the ability to stop the process safely, the discharge route and the maintenance plan. Continuous operation alone does not prove that a self-cleaning separator is appropriate. Likewise, occasional contamination does not remove the need for safe access and a defined cleaning procedure. The project team should document the reason for the chosen arrangement. Environmental conditions can change the final equipment details without changing the basic process objective. Outdoor exposure, coastal corrosion, high dust levels, rain, ambient temperature, altitude and transport constraints may affect finishes, guards, electrical coordination and support design.
